Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-03

Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Summerset - Head of ML), Alex Ryder (Summerset - SRE), Benji Park (Summerset - Product), Lina Cho (Summerset - Data Eng)

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're on for about 45 minutes. I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, and with me is Diego from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
00:07 Priya: Good, thanks. Excited — we want to understand how to lower inference costs for our chat assistant and also keep tail latency within 300 ms.
00:12 Benji: Yeah hi all.
00:14 Alex: Hello.
00:20 Diego: Cool, quick agenda: we will show the Optimize console recommendations, run a couple of cost sims for your traffic profiles, and then discuss pilot scope. We'll focus on prefix/KV prefetch because Priya had mentioned long session contexts.
00:32 Priya: Right, our sessions average 1.8k tokens but heavy tails to 6k for some users.
00:39 Diego: Got it. That kind of distribution strongly benefits from session KV. We call KV/prefix prefetch — sometimes the transcript tool says K V cache — but basically precomputing the prefix KV to avoid re-encoding.
00:50 Maya: Also we'll contrast hosted API vs Dedicated capacity numbers.
00:55 Benji: Quick clarifying Q: what's the recommended concurrency for our latency SLO? We currently run 50 concurrent connections fronting an NGINX LB.
01:05 Diego: Short answer: it depends on the mix of short vs long requests. Our sim tool estimates cost across concurrency values. We'll run their histogram in the demo.
01:12 Alex: Also security — we need to know data residency and KMS options for key management.
01:18 Maya: Yep we'll cover that at the end and share doc links.
01:22 Diego: Okay I'll share my screen — switching to Optimize console. (small pause) I apologize if resolution is fuzzy — screen share.
01:40 Diego: Here is the model catalog — for this demo we picked an open medium-latency family, the 13B quantized variant you mentioned in the form. On the right, Optimize suggests prefetch and batching knobs based on your request profile. The important bits: prefix prefetch hit rate, average token reuse, and concurrency targets.
02:05 Priya: How do you estimate prefix hit rate? Our app sometimes stitches third-party context so the prefix isn't always identical.
02:14 Diego: Good point. The hit rate estimation comes from token-level overlap between session starts. If you have dynamic third-party context, effective hit rate drops — in practice we'd run a pilot to measure actual prefix stability. You can supply request traces.
02:28 Priya: We can share anon traces — we'll scrub PII.
02:32 Diego: Perfect. I'm switching to the cost simulation tab — this is the same sim we used in our internal playbooks.
02:40 Diego: (typing) Uploading sample histogram... the console accepts a token histogram CSV or a short JSON with percentiles.
02:50 Benji: If we prefetch KV, does that increase memory usage on the serving nodes? Does it require heavier GPUs?
02:59 Diego: Prefetch increases per-session KV cache storage; it's mostly RAM and GPU VRAM depending on KV format. We offer quantization-friendly KV storage which makes it smaller, but yeah there's a memory vs cost tradeoff. For many cases prefetch reduces per-token compute enough to net savings.
03:20 Alex: What's the fallback if KV prefetch misses? Does latency spike?
03:24 Diego: If miss, we fall back to full encode for the prefix which adds the prefix compute—so you see added latency on that first request. The console lets you model miss rates and shows expected latency percentiles.
03:34 Maya: I'm switching the sim to Summerset's numbers — Diego, use 1.8k mean with 6k tail.
03:42 Diego: Doing it now. (short pause, clicking) Uploaded. The sim runs a batch sweep across concurrency and batch size.
04:00 Diego: Results: with aggressive prefix prefetch (80% hit), cost per 1k tokens drops ~28% vs no prefetch at median concurrency 40. At 95th tail, latency remains within 320 ms only if we cap batch windows (we show an example cap = 20 ms).
04:22 Priya: Hmm 320 ms is slightly above our 300 ms SLO. Can we tune batch windows?
04:27 Diego: Yes, reduce batch wait to 10 ms or use lower concurrency with more instances. That will raise nominal cost a bit but tighten tail latency. The console shows the tradeoff curve.
04:38 Benji: How does Dedicated compare here? If we move to Dedicated reserved capacity, do we get better tail performance?
04:46 Diego: Dedicated gives more predictable latency since you control concurrency per GPU and avoid noisy neighbors. Economic math: Dedicated is cheaper if you have sustained throughput. The sim includes a Dedicated break-even line — for your profile it looks like Dedicated becomes attractive at about X tokens per minute. I'll send the exact breakout.
05:05 Maya: Note: our Dedicated pricing sheet is in the deck — I'll attach after the call.
05:12 Lina: A quick infra Q — we use GKE and private VPC. How does the private deployment work for us?
05:18 Maya: Redwood Private can run in your VPC with customer-managed network peering and KMS integration. There is an on-prem option if needed. We'll share the private deployment checklist.
05:26 Alex: Great.
05:28 Diego: Back to the sim — I'm toggling prefetch formats. We support full prefix KV (best hit rate, larger memory), lightweight fingerprints (smaller memory, slightly lower hit), and sessionization hybrid. Each has a different cost curve.
05:44 Priya: Which do you recommend for chat assistants with lots of short QA-style requests vs long docs?
05:51 Diego: For mixed workloads, session hybrid is nice — keep fingerprints for short quick requests, and full KV for active long sessions. The console will auto-suggest per-route policies.
06:04 Benji: Is the routing per customer or per route? We want different policies for our search augmentation vs multi-turn chat.
06:12 Diego: Per-route policies. You can pin route A to prefetch-heavy and route B to low-latency small-batch.
06:18 Priya: About model fallbacks — if my preferred model is unavailable do you auto-fallback to a smaller variant? How does that affect tokenization and KV compatibility?
06:27 Diego: We can auto-fallback to compatible model families; KV formats are model dependent though. You can configure graceful fallback policies that either re-encode or use model-variant-compatible caches. In some cases we prefer to roll to a quantized variant of same arch.
06:41 Alex: Do you support HSM KMS for key wrapping? We need to show auditors.
06:46 Maya: Yes we integrate with customer KMS and HSM via the private plane in Dedicated/Private. We'll send the compliance doc link.
06:53 Priya: Okay the numbers you showed — is the 28% savings after allowing for increased KV storage costs?
06:59 Diego: The sim factors in storage costs, extra instance requirements for KV storage, and the reduced per-token compute. For your histogram the net is ~28% at 80% hit. At 50% hit the savings drop to ~10%.
07:15 Benji: Can we run an actual bench using our traffic so we can validate hit rates?
07:20 Maya: Yes that is the pilot we'll propose. Diego, outline the pilot scope — what do we need from Summerset?
07:27 Diego: Pilot scope: 1) Summerset provides 48 hours of anonymized request traces + token histograms; 2) Redwood runs a 4-hour benchmark in our sandbox configured to mirror peak concurrency windows; 3) we return a per-route cost breakdown and suggested policies. Expected turnaround ~7 business days from trace receipt.
07:44 Priya: Sounds good. We'll get traces by next Thursday.
07:48 Alex: On SSO — we need SAML + SCIM for user provisioning to the console.
07:52 Maya: We support SAML and SCIM; CSM will kick in with the integration doc.
07:56 Benji: Any gotchas on token counting differences? Our instrumentation sometimes double counts trailing tokens.
08:03 Diego: We recommend a canonical tokenizer-based counting during the pilot. We'll also include a reconciliation script.
08:10 (short silence while Diego tweaks console)
08:25 Diego: New sim view — here's a heatmap of cost vs concurrency and prefetch hit. Dark zones are cheaper. See how the 40-60 concurrency band with 70-85% hit is the sweet spot.
08:40 Priya: How do you get to 70-85% hit in practice?
08:43 Diego: Techniques: standardize session prefixes, normalize third-party context, or short-circuit retrieving vendor context and include it as part of the session to increase repeatability. Also TTL-based prefetch for semi-static prefixes.
09:00 Priya: That might require product changes. We expected some engineering work.
09:04 Benji: We'll need cost/benefit to justify that work.
09:07 Maya: The cost sim helps with that. We'll show estimated payback in weeks if you implement prefix normalization.
09:14 Priya: What's the typical payback we've seen?
09:17 Diego: Varies. For heavy-session apps — 6-10 weeks; for mixed workloads longer. We'll include a payback calc in the spreadsheet.
09:26 Alex: Are there any licensing constraints for open models you recommend?
09:30 Diego: We curate open models and annotate licensing in the catalog. We'll flag any downstream use restrictions.
09:35 Benji: Can we whiteboard a small example? Suppose 2k token prefix repeats 60% of time, average generation 200 tokens. Show numbers roughly.
09:45 Diego: Sure. (typing) If prefix encode costs X ms and generation costs Y ms per token, the prefetch amortizes prefix cost across hits. For your numbers, net compute reduction per session is roughly 0.6 * prefix_cost - prefetch_storage_overhead amortized. That maps to the sim numbers I showed earlier.
10:10 Priya: Fine. Switching topics — reporting and per-token billing transparency? We need token-level breakdown for chargeback across product teams.
10:18 Maya: Redwood Console includes per-route token cost and per-token breakdown, with exportable CSV and token-level traces (anonymized on request).
10:27 Alex: Good.
10:29 Benji: Any reference artifacts?
10:31 Maya: I'll drop the Optimize playbook deck, pricing worksheet, and the Dedicated pricing matrix. Also SOC2 and private deployment checklist. Links: (1) deck: https://redwood.ai/decks/optimize-playbook (2) pricing sheet: https://redwood.ai/pricing/dedicated-worksheet (these are short links for reference).
10:52 Priya: Perfect.
10:55 Diego: Quick demo of a live run — I'm spinning up a small sandbox sim to show per-request traces and how prefix hits are recorded. (short pause) You can see these green markers where prefix hit occurred.
11:18 Priya: Nice. Does the dashboard let us tune rollouts per route?
11:22 Diego: Yes, you can A/B split, set canary thresholds, and define auto-fallback to lower-capacity variants.
11:28 Benji: For the pilot, do we need to sign any additional agreements?
11:32 Maya: Standard pilot agreement (non-prod SLA) — we'll send a one-pager.
11:36 Alex: How long does it take to stand up the sandbox?
11:39 Diego: For this sim we used an existing sandbox — for a dedicated pilot you'd need network whitelisting, which can be done in 3-5 business days typically.
11:48 Priya: Okay great.
11:50 Maya: Quick recap and next steps — Priya will share traces by 2026-05-07, Maya will send pricing and pilot agreement by 2026-05-05, Diego will run the sim and return detailed CSV by 2026-05-10. Any other blockers?
12:06 Priya: Not from me.
12:09 Benji: No.
12:10 Alex: No.
12:12 Maya: Awesome. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email and attach the artifacts.
